## Vignette

**Chief complaint:** Black stools for three days

**History:** Brought in by his grandparents, whom he is visiting: for three days he has passed one dark, black, semi-formed stool a day and has complained intermittently of abdominal pain, from which he is easily distracted. No vomiting, reduced appetite, drooling, swallowing difficulty, cough, stridor or breathlessness. He is minimally verbal, so the history is limited. On further questioning he is known to eat non-food items, regularly including sand, and three days ago he came home from nursery with a dark blue-stained tongue, thought to be from ink or pigment.

- **Past history:** Awaiting assessment for autism; minimally verbal and follows only a few commands; Chronic constipation; Eats non-food items (pica), including sand
- **Medications:** Daily herbal multivitamin and probiotic supplements (limited diet)
- **Allergies:** No known drug allergies †
- **Social:** Visiting his grandparents, who brought him in; attends nursery.

## Vitals on arrival

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 158/min | 96 †/58 † mm Hg | 26/min † | 99% † | 36.8 °C (98.2 °F) † | — |

## Examination

- Actively playing in the department; distressed by having observations taken
- No acute abnormality: airway, breathing and circulation normal
- Abdomen non-tender
- Examination limited by his communication difficulties
- Stool (photographed by family): black, semi-formed; consistent with melena or pigment staining

## Imaging

- **Abdominal radiograph (single view):** 21.9 mm round radio-opaque object in the stomach with a halo sign; a second 9.4 mm radio-opaque object in the right iliac fossa. The film did not include the pelvis.

## Diagnosis

**Button battery ingestion (unwitnessed) with a 21.9 mm battery retained in the stomach and melena** (ICD-10-CM T18.2XXA / K92.1)

Differentials: Black stool from ingested pigment, iron or bismuth; Peptic ulcer bleeding; Meckel diverticulum; Other ingested foreign body (coins, magnets)

## Management

1. Discussed with the regional pediatric surgical team and transferred within 190 minutes of triage
2. Endoscopic retrieval within 6 h of triage (rat-tooth, then Magill forceps); no significant tissue injury apart from mild erythema at the pylorus
3. Observed overnight and discharged with advice to return if symptoms persisted

## Outcome

Doing well since discharge; the melena resolved.

## Teaching points

- Suspect unwitnessed foreign-body ingestion in young, nonverbal or developmentally delayed children, especially with pica, unexplained GI bleeding, food refusal, drooling or respiratory symptoms.
- Image the whole tract, from nasopharynx to anus, ideally in two views; a halo (double-ring) outline on the frontal view and a step-off on the lateral view distinguish a button battery from a coin (thin batteries may lack the halo).
- An esophageal button battery is an emergency: remove it immediately, ideally within 2 hours, because hydroxide generated at the negative pole causes liquefactive necrosis within hours.
- Honey (from 1 year of age) or sucralfate can limit esophageal injury while removal of a recent ingestion (within 12 h) is arranged, without delaying it (National Capital Poison Center guideline); neither is indicated once the battery is known to be beyond the esophagus (ESPGHAN 2021 position paper).
- Batteries beyond the esophagus usually pass, but a symptomatic child needs endoscopic removal and assessment for injury (ESPGHAN 2021 position paper).

## Quiz questions

### Q1 · next-step

Given his history of eating non-food items, which imaging is most appropriate?

- A. Abdominal ultrasound
- B. Abdominal radiograph alone
- **C. Radiographs from the nasopharynx to the anus** ✓
- D. CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

*Why:* For a suspected radio-opaque foreign body, radiographs should cover the whole tract from the nasopharynx to the anus, with a lateral view of any object, so that an esophageal battery or a second object is not missed; this child's single abdominal film omitted the pelvis. Ultrasound and CT are not first-line.

### Q2 · interpretation

What is the 21.9 mm gastric object most likely to be?

> Abdominal radiograph: a 21.9 mm round radio-opaque object in the stomach whose edge shows a double-ring (halo) outline, and a 9.4 mm radio-opaque object in the right iliac fossa.

- **A. A button (lithium coin-cell) battery** ✓
- B. A single coin
- C. Two stacked magnets
- D. A metal washer

*Why:* A double-ring (halo) outline on the frontal view, with a step-off on the lateral view, is the classic sign of a button battery; a coin is a uniformly dense disc and a washer has a central hole. Stacked coins can mimic the halo, so treat it as a battery until proven otherwise.

### Q3 · management

What is the most appropriate management?

> Battery in the stomach; time of ingestion unknown (stools black for 3 days). Hemoglobin 113 g/L (reference 115–140); coagulation and renal function normal.

- A. Discharge with a repeat radiograph in 7–14 days
- B. Polyethylene glycol to speed passage, then stool checks
- C. Honey every 10 minutes and overnight observation
- **D. Urgent referral for endoscopic removal** ✓

*Why:* Most batteries beyond the esophagus pass, but this child is symptomatic (melena, abdominal pain, mild anemia) after an unknown, possibly prolonged exposure to a cell over 20 mm, so prompt endoscopic removal and assessment for injury are indicated (ESPGHAN 2021 position paper). Honey is for recent ingestions while an esophageal battery awaits removal, not for a gastric battery.

### Q4 · risk

Which scenario carries the greatest risk of severe injury after button battery ingestion?

- A. A battery under 15 mm that has reached the colon
- **B. A 20 mm lithium cell lodged in the esophagus of a toddler** ✓
- C. A zinc-air hearing-aid battery in a teenager's stomach
- D. A battery passed in the stool within 24 hours

*Why:* Severe and fatal outcomes cluster in children under 5 with 20 mm-plus, 3-V lithium cells impacted in the esophagus, where hydroxide generated at the negative pole causes necrosis within about 2 hours and can lead to perforation, tracheoesophageal or aortoesophageal fistula and vocal cord paralysis. Small batteries beyond the esophagus usually pass without harm.
